transcription.tex: We will study the definition and purpose of hyperbolic functions, such as \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\), their inverses, and how to manipulate, differentiate and integrate them.\par 1. Definitions and sketches: find the exact value of \(\tanh(\ln4)\).\par 2. Inverse functions: prove \(\operatorname{arcosh}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})\).

3. Identities and equations: solve \(2\cosh^2x-5\sinh x=5\) for real \(x\).\par 4. Differentiation: determine \(\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{arsinh}(\sqrt{x})\).\par 5. Integration: determine \(\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{12x+2x^2}}\,dx\).

transcription.tex: Each hyperbolic function has an inverse. Use the prefix “ar”, as in arsinh (not arcsinh).\par The six inverses are\[\operatorname{arsinh}x,\ \operatorname{arcosh}x,\ \operatorname{artanh}x,\]\[\operatorname{arsech}x,\ \operatorname{arcosech}x,\ \operatorname{arcoth}x.\]

transcription.tex: Why is there a problem finding the inverse of \(f(x)=\cosh x\)?\par A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one. Unrestricted \(\cosh x\) is many-to-one, so reflecting its whole graph would give a one-to-many relation.\par Restrict \(x\ge0\). Then reflect in \(y=x\) to get \(y=\operatorname{arcosh}x\), with domain \(x\ge1\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Hyperbolic functions are exponential, so their inverses can be expressed using logarithms.\par Prove \(\operatorname{arsinh}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1})\).
\[e^y=\frac{2x\pm\sqrt{4x^2+4}}2=x\pm\sqrt{x^2+1}.\]Since \(\sqrt{x^2+1}>|x|\) and \(e^y>0\), only the positive sign is possible.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: \[y=\operatorname{arcosh}x\Rightarrow x=\cosh y=\frac{e^y+e^{-y}}2\]\[e^y+e^{-y}=2x\Rightarrow e^{2y}-2xe^y+1=0.\]\[a=1,\ b=-2x,\ c=1\]\[e^y=\frac{2x\pm\sqrt{4x^2-4}}2=x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}.\]Both roots are positive, but the principal inverse has \(y\ge0\). Thus\[y=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}).\]
Show why the other logarithm is non-positive.
\[(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})=1\]\[x-\sqrt{x^2-1}=\frac1{x+\sqrt{x^2-1}}\]\[\ln(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})=-\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})\le0.\]Equality occurs only at \(x=1\), where both branches give zero.

transcription.tex: Textbook\par (a) Show \(\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{arsinh}x=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}\). We did this earlier.\par (b) Find the first two non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion.\par Given\[\operatorname{arsinh}x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n(2n)!}{2^{2n}(n!)^2}\frac{x^{2n+1}}{2n+1},\quad |x|<1,\]\par (c) Find the coefficient of \(x^5\).\par (d) Use terms up to \(x^5\) to approximate \(\operatorname{arsinh}0.5\).\par (e) Calculate the percentage error.

\[f(x)=\operatorname{arsinh}x,\quad f(0)=0\]\[f^{\prime}(x)=(1+x^2)^{-1/2},\quad f^{\prime}(0)=1\]\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=-x(1+x^2)^{-3/2},\quad f^{\prime\prime}(0)=0\]\[f^{\prime\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{2x^2-1}{(1+x^2)^{5/2}},\quad f^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)=-1.\]Continue until two non-zero terms appear:\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)}{3!}x^3+\cdots\]\[\operatorname{arsinh}x\approx x-\frac{x^3}{6}.\]

transcription.tex: Find \(\int\cosh^5(2x)\sinh(2x)\,dx\).\par Recall the “consider and scale” method used for \(\int\sin^n x\cos x\,dx\) and \(\int\cos^n x\sin x\,dx\).
Find \(\int\tanh x\,dx\).\par As for ordinary tan, first express the function as a quotient.
\[\int\tanh x\,dx=\int\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}\,dx\]\[=\ln|\cosh x|+C.\]There is no minus sign: cosh differentiates to positive sinh. Also \(\cosh x>0\), so the modulus can be omitted.

Use \(x=a\sinh u\). The denominator becomes \(a\cosh u\) and \(dx=a\cosh u\,du\), so they cancel.\par With \(x=a\tan\theta\), the denominator gives \(a\sec\theta\) but \(dx=a\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), leaving an extra sec factor.

transcription.tex: Show \(\int\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}x+\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+C\).\par Hint: use a sensible substitution. Recall \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\), \(1+\sinh^2u=\cosh^2u\).

Try \(x=\tan\theta\), \(-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2\):\[dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta,\quad I=\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta.\]Integrate by parts with \(u=\sec\theta\), \(dv/d\theta=\sec^2\theta\), hence \(du/d\theta=\sec\theta\tan\theta\), \(v=\tan\theta\):\[I=\sec\theta\tan\theta-\int\sec\theta\tan^2\theta\,d\theta\]\[=\sec\theta\tan\theta-\int\sec\theta(\sec^2\theta-1)\,d\theta\]\[=\sec\theta\tan\theta-I+\int\sec\theta\,d\theta.\]\[2I=\sec\theta\tan\theta+\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C\]\[I=\tfrac12\sec\theta\tan\theta+\tfrac12\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C\]\[=\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\tfrac12\ln|\sqrt{1+x^2}+x|+C\]\[=\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}x+C.\]

Try \(x=\sinh u\):\[dx=\cosh u\,du\]\[I=\int\cosh u\cosh u\,du=\int\cosh^2u\,du\]\[=\tfrac12\int(1+\cosh2u)\,du\]\[=\tfrac12\left(u+\tfrac12\sinh2u\right)+C\]\[=\tfrac12u+\tfrac12\sinh u\cosh u+C\]\[=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}x+\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+C.\]This substitution gives the shorter method.
